books.section: Topic 5.9 Government Policies During the Civil War
Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Thirteenth Amendment to the Constitution (ratified December 6, 1865)

stimulus.source_note: Thirteenth Amendment to the Constitution, proposed by Congress January 31, 1865, ratified December 6, 1865. Public domain. Wording verified against the Constitution Annotated text.
stimulus.text:
“Section 1. Neither slavery nor involuntary servitude, except as a punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly convicted, shall exist within the United States, or any place subject to their jurisdiction.

Section 2. Congress shall have power to enforce this article by appropriate legislation.”

—Thirteenth Amendment, as ratified December 6, 1865

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The amendment was proposed by Congress in early 1865 and ratified on December 6, 1865. Its ratification completed a change that began with the Emancipation Proclamation, because the proclamation

options.text: had already freed every enslaved person in the whole country by itself.

rationales.A: Background: the proclamation left slavery in the loyal border states untouched.
rationales.B: Background: the proclamation was a presidential war order, not a constitutional amendment.
rationales.C: Background: the proclamation applied to states and parts of states in rebellion, and expressly left the border states out.
rationales.D: The proclamation was a wartime order reaching only rebel territory, so only the amendment made freedom permanent and nationwide.
rationales.general:
1. Trace the change in two steps: order first, amendment second.
2. The order was a war measure, tied to rebellion and to the president’s war power.
3. War measures can be questioned or undone when the war ends.
4. The amendment writes freedom into the Constitution, where no president can erase it.
Remember: an order does the work of the moment, and an amendment locks the work in place.
